extracted.intended_audience: American patrons of art, artists, and educated readers interested in art criticism and public monuments
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on evaluating painters and sculptors, the qualities of good art, and proper patronage (including costs, selection of public monuments, and study abroad). Emphasizes originality, composition, execution, and fair treatment/payment of artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace and faithful modeling versus originality and heartfelt message
rubrics_metrics.description: Terry loves grace, and consciously works from the model. The result is a pleasing transposition of the hues of this clime. But the design of the picture is never original, nor is it laden with any message from, the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasing grace and faithful workmanship (a true rendering from the model) are valuable, but should not substitute for original design or emotional/message-bearing content. Beware artists whose technique is charming yet whose compositions lack originality or heartfelt meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality, poetic heart, and studied coloring (Hicks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Hicks I think very highly. He is a man of ideas, an original observer, and with a poetic heart. His system of coloring is derived from a thoughtful study, not a mere imitation of nature, and shows the fineness of his organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value artists who are original observers and who develop a system of coloring from thoughtful study rather than mere imitation. Such organization and poetic sensibility indicate higher artistic promise; they may need competent patronage to realize larger works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between detailed natural study and poetic feeling (Cropsey vs Cranch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cropsey is a reverent and careful student of nature in detail; it is no pedantry, but a true love he has, and his pictures are full of little, gentle signs of intimacy. They please and touch; but yet in poetic feeling of the heart of nature he is not equal to Cranch, who produces fine effects by means more superficial, and, on examination, less satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good landscape painting requires both intimate, reverent study of natural detail and a deeper poetic feeling for the spirit of nature. An ideal artist may combine Cropsey's fidelity to detail with Cranch's poetic effect; each trait has strengths and weaknesses and artists might profitably learn from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfusion of spirit beyond mere copies
rubrics_metrics.description: I hope to see, not only copies upon canvas of our magnificent scenes, but a transfusion of the spirit which is their divinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscapes should do more than copy scenes literally; the successful painter conveys the spirit or divinity of the place. Original, interpretive treatment that captures mood and spiritual quality is a higher aim than photographic reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Italian study for learning composition (union of variety and harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruins of Italy, in their varied relations with vegetation and the heavens, make speeches from every stone for instruction of the artist; the greatest variety here is found with the greatest harmony. To know how this union may be accomplished is a main secret of art...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few years' study in Italy is valuable because it exposes the artist to examples where variety and harmony are successfully united. Learning how to achieve such compositional union is a central lesson of artistic training, and can instruct the eye for other climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture as a natural province for Americans (permanence and relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The permanence of material and solid, relief in the forms correspond to the positiveness of his nature better than the mere ephemeral and even tricky methods of the painter,--to his need of motion and action, better than the chambered scribbling of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture's solidity and permanence are particularly well suited to the American character and historical subjects; sculptors can record national facts and ideals in durable form that aligns with national temperament and public architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and spirit in portrait-busts; idealized character-types (Story, Mozier)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fidelity and spirit of his portrait-busts could be appreciated by every one; for an ideal head of Pocahontas, too, he had at once orders for many copies. It was not an Indian head, but, in the union of sweetness and strength with a princelike, childlike dignity, very happily expressive of his idea of her character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful portrait-busts combine faithful characterization with expressive spirit; idealized heads that capture a conceived character (sweetness, dignity, strength) can be popular and widely ordered. Execution and conception both matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal expression and plastic power; depth of artistic thought (assessment of Powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: I consider the Slave as a form of simple and sweet beauty, but that neither as an ideal expression nor a specimen of plastic power is it transcendent. Powers stands far higher in his busts than in any ideal statue... his conception of what is individual in character is clear and just, his power of execution almost unrivalled; but he has had a lifetime of discipline for the bust, while his studies on the human body are comparatively limited; nor is his treatment of it free and masterly. To me, his conception of subject is not striking: I do not consider him rich in artistic thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating figurative sculpture, consider: (1) ideal expression (is the subject elevated/idealized?), (2) plastic power (command of form in three dimensions), (3) anatomical study and freedom in treatment of the body, and (4) richness of conception. Strong execution in one genre (busts) does not guarantee success in ideal or full-figure works without adequate study and conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and harmony of public groups; effective distant silhouette
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine work of art will always have, at a distance, where its details cannot be discerned, a beautiful effect, as of architectural ornament... He would have been pleased with the beautiful balance of forms in this group, with the freedom with which light and air play in and out, the management of the whole being clear and satisfactory at the first glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public sculpture and groups should be composed so they read well at distance: balanced forms, clear overall management, harmonious interaction of figures and accessories, and pleasing play of light and air. First impressions at a distance are as important as detailed studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of allegory/support figures in a group (winged Fame example)
rubrics_metrics.description: He has represented Washington in his actual dress; a figure of Fame, winged, presents the laurel and civic wreath; his gesture declines them... This group has no insipid, allegorical air... The angel figure is draped, and with the liberty-cap... seems to connect the two figures, and in an artistic point of view balances well the cocked hat; there is a similar harmony between the angel's wings and the extremities of the horse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical figures can provide poetic sense, structural support, and compositional balance if treated without insipidity. They should relate naturally to the principal figure and help induce appropriate action and harmony in the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process for public monuments: impartial judges and open concurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignified way to manage that affair would be to have a committee chosen of impartial judges, men who would look only to the merits of the work and the interests of the country, unbiassed by any personal interest in favor of some one artist... let each artist offer his design for an equestrian statue of Washington, and let the best have the preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public commissions should be awarded by impartial committees focused solely on artistic merit and public interest. Open competitions where each artist submits a design allow fair comparison and best selection; exclude nepotism, jockeying, and personal biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist compensation must include design time and overhead (patron obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: He does not consider that the painter, the sculptor, must be paid for the time he spends in designing and moulding, no less than in painting and carving; that he must have his bread and sleeping-house, his workhouse or studio, his marbles and colors,--the sculptor his workmen; so that if the price be paid he asks, a modest and delicate man very commonly receives _no_ guerdon for his thought,--the real essence of the work,--except the luxury of seeing it embodied, which he could not otherwise have afforded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should understand and fairly compensate the full costs of artistic production: the artist's design time, living, studio, materials, and assistants. Undervaluing these costs robs the artist of the most important element—the thought and conception behind the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper patron conduct: do not change orders or unduly bargainthe artist
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Mæcenas sometimes, after ordering a work, has been known to change his mind when the statue is already modelled. The American Mæcenas often pushes the price down... from a habit of making what are called good bargains... bargains for one's own advantage at the expense of a poorer brother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should not rescind or change commissions after models are complete, nor bargain down prices out of ignorance or habit. Such behavior is cruel to artists who have invested thought and labor; fair dealing and understanding of process are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cost benchmarks for sculpture and study abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent of a suitable studio for modelling in clay and executing statues in marble may be estimated at $200 a year. The best journeyman carver in marble at Rome receives $60 a month. Models are paid $1 a day. As a general guide... for a statue of life-size the demand is from $1,000 to $5,000... $1,000 per annum should be placed at the disposal of every young artist leaving our country for Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide patrons and students with concrete cost expectations (studio rent, wages, model rates, price ranges for statues) and recommend adequate study funding (around $1,000/year) to avoid the false notion that study in Italy is cheap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine enthusiasm elevates; writing/talking for effect debases
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine enthusiasm, however crude the state of mind from which it springs, always elevates, always educates; but in the same proportion talking and writing for effect stultifies and debases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authentic, heartfelt enthusiasm for art. Beware of mere fashion, drawing-room rapture, or newspaper echo; publicity for effect can stultify appreciation and lead to inflated but hollow acclaim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic legitimacy principle: recognize governments chosen by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity way... would be to recognize for any nation the government chosen by itself. The suffrage had been correct here... The Roman people claims once more to have a national existence. It declines further serfdom to an ecclesiastical court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a political standard (expressed in the essay), a republican nation should recognize another nation's government when it is chosen by that nation's people and can sustain itself. This is offered as the 'only respectable' position for a republican government.
